What it does not do It doesn't migrate data. It has no offline mode, no Turso Cloud and no R2 replication. It drops subtasks, task links, workstreams, ADRs, facts, plan revisions, owner grants, stand-downs and thread refilings. It adds no database kinds beyond central and workspace, no workflow engine, and no advisor machinery. Deliverable assets in R2 come later. Sign-in, the proxy and production stay untouched until you give the go-ahead.

Requirements: workspace storage redesign This page has to answer one question first: what is this redesign for, and what's inside or outside it? The needs are written once you confirm the two lists below.

What's inside the redesign, and what isn't This is the boundary every need has to stay within. Proposed: I assembled it from your decisions (`owner-decisions.md`), and it needs your explicit confirmation. Field Boundary Goal "The router just works." Collaboration storage becomes simple: one central per org plus one database per workspace, with the replication, project locks and the earlier cruft removed. Who it affects You (the owner and operator); the agents using board, mail and automation tools through the CLI and MCP; each Mac's Router; and the Fleet access Lead's sign-in, which talks to central. What to reuse Central's core, with its Cloudflare and Tokio hosts; the SQLx Durable Object driver; mail in central; the Router's local stores; and the agent tool surface, reshaped where entities change. What becomes different Central holds machines, auth, the workspaces list, all agent messages, and automations and wakes. Each workspace has one database holding its areas, projects and all their content. Macs keep no project files, no sync and no project locks. Every host uses SQLite through SQLx, and every migration is SQLx. The organization follows capabilities C1–C8 above. Notifications are redesigned in central. May change codex-router , plus the parts of agent-fleet-sync it uses. Protected Production, until you give the go-ahead; the proxy (AGENTS.md); sign-in and switchboard. Not doing No data migration: the new system starts empty, and old data is backed up for you to pick from later. No offline mode, no Turso Cloud, no R2 replication. No subtasks, workstreams, ADRs, facts, plan revisions, owner grants, stand-downs or refilings. No database kinds beyond central and workspace. No workflow engine (the old one is ripped out). No Cloudflare Worker crons without your OK. How we'll know it's done On staging with two Macs: agents create, post, read, get notified and message each other across machines, and a new Mac works after only enrolling. Still open The decisions on the home page : version history, which notifications to keep, where the actor list lives, and whether the SDK code moves into codex-router . The needs and obligations must stay inside it. Anything outside it comes back to you as a decision. Comment on the row that's wrong, or on this choice. Answer both, then use Comments' Copy and paste the result to me.

Central execution model: Program Design One engine core, written as event handlers over storage, runs unchanged on Tokio and on Cloudflare workers-rs. Each shell implements one platform contract: storage, the alarm (lower-only inside a transaction, exact in one serialized recompute), sockets with attachments, clock and ids, an event-scoped deadline, and calls to other objects. Every event opens the object once, handles its own units in short transactions, runs due work if the cadence allows, recomputes the alarm in one serialized section, and returns. Nothing the object needs lives only in memory, and no timer or wait outlives its event, so a Durable Object hibernates with every Router still connected. Every request may go as a batch, an ordered array of one type; every request and answer carries a UUIDv7 send_id , which is how answers find their attempt row. The notice acknowledgment is specified (wire, storage, delivery, released Routers). agent-fleet-sync's owed-row writes return OwedChange and central writes the attempt rows ( boundary ). A push retired without an answer is Uncertain . The cutover list is complete. These close Opus's revision-4 findings V4-1 to V4-6. All attempt and failure state moves into one table, central_work_attempts ( below ), keyed by the subject's UUIDv7 and a short kind; repeated failures are retired after 24 h; no existing table gains attempt columns; two agent-fleet-sync tables get UUIDv7 keys. Also: call events hand due work to the alarm (Sol 16), and the feed read uses an effective floor (Sol 17). Opus (19 findings) and Sol (10 findings) reviewed revision 2 independently; every finding is accepted. Biggest changes: answers are matched by the frame id stored on the row, not the effect id (the wire carries only the frame id); owed work is split into four kinds by who answers it; the delivery report is the Router's, not central's; the alarm has one serialized recompute plus a lower-only operation; an event-scoped deadline stays in the contract; failing due work keeps its backoff and error in one small failures table (your decision); Fleet feed retention and Copy staged-part expiry are due sources; migration and initialization are a contained step 0. Finding-by-finding: review disposition .

Three rules that make hibernation safe Rule Means Checked by H1. Storage is the truth; memory is a cache Anything that must survive is a row, the alarm, or a socket attachment. Memory may keep only caches rebuilt from storage, hints whose loss costs extra work (never wrong behavior), and state scoped to one running event Journeys pass with the object rebuilt at every quiescent point (R18) H2. No timer outlives its event The alarm is the only timer that survives an event. Inside an event, a wait may have a deadline (an event-scoped timer, cancelled when the event ends). Nothing waits in memory for a later event After each event: no pending task or timer other than the Tokio shell's alarm timer; on Cloudflare, hibernation observed (R17) H3. Keepalive never wakes the object Routers use websocket protocol Ping. Cloudflare answers it with an automatic Pong, doesn't call the handler and doesn't bill it ( facts ) Keepalive-caused invocations are zero (R19)

Requests that start a long operation Today Register, Claim, owner move and takeover, admin import, retirement and enrollment each call engine.drive_due() before answering ( registry_lease_calls.rs:117 , owner_registry_runtime.rs:86, 150 , admin_import_registry.rs:88 , machine_enrollment.rs:160 , owner_retirement.rs:72 , copy_write_calls.rs:297 ). That runs every due operation, including someone else's move waiting on a silent holder, so one request can wait behind another's operation. New: these handlers start their operation and drive only that operation , through a new drive_one(operation) in durable-steps, bounded by event_deadline . Then they answer with today's wire answers: Register Registered / Refused , or the answer is lost and the Router retries the same attempt if the operation is still running; Claim Pending{transfer} or its outcome. Every other operation is driven by the due batch.

One table for every attempt: central_work_attempts (your decision) Every retryable thing (a push being resent, a status message, a summary call, a session close, a cleanup item that keeps failing) has the same state: is it in flight, when to try next, how many tries, the last error. Revision 3 repeated those columns on five tables and added a failures table. Revision 4 keeps them in one table per object store , and existing tables don't change. Name: central_ , the prefix central already uses for engine bookkeeping that every object store carries ( central_schema_migrations , central_schema_migration_failures in migration_bookkeeping.rs ). Domain tables are named by domain ( fleet_ , machine_ , lease_ ); _copy_ is the Copy object's internals; _fleet_sync_ is agent-fleet-sync's. Column Meaning id (key, UUIDv7) The attempt subject (UUIDv7) The primary key of the row being attempted: mail item, status row, Copy summary, claim reservation, session ( _fleet_sync_sessions.id ), a machine's notice progress row ( notice_delivery and notice_expiry run per machine, machine_notice_store.rs:198–215 ), feed state, staged part. Every subject table is keyed by a UUIDv7 ( two agent-fleet-sync tables need one added ) kind What is being attempted on it: push , status , summary_call , settlement , session_close , notice_delivery , notice_expiry , mail_retention , feed_retention , part_expiry , forward_expiry , lease . Unique together with subject , because one row can have two attempts (a mail item's push and its 60-day removal) state waiting · in_flight · given_up send_id , connection_id , session_id , sent_version Socket requests only: the UUIDv7 send id every answer echoes, and the latest send's connection, for answer matching and the window count next_attempt_at , attempts Backoff: 30 s doubling, cap 10 min first_failed_at , last_error_class , last_error For health and retirement No row unless something is pending or failing. A healthy object's table is nearly empty. A row is created in the same transaction as the work it tracks, and deleted in the transaction that finishes it. Owners find their own rows by joining on their table ( JOIN _fleet_sync_outbox_items o ON o.item_id = a.subject ). The table never decides what runs: each owner still does its own work, one item per unit. One query each for the scheduler's earliest retry ( MIN(next_attempt_at) where state != given_up ), the window count ( in_flight on a connection) and answer matching ( send_id ). Domain deadlines stay on their rows. "Expire this notice after 7 days" is the notice's own expires_at . A central_work_attempts row appears for it only if expiring it fails. Failures with no row of their own (step 0 open, a source's next-due read, the alarm write, a handler that rolled back) use the object itself as subject: a Copy object's DatabaseId (UUIDv7, replication_ids.rs:59–61 ); the Fleet object, which has no address id ( ObjectAddress::Fleet ), uses the state_id of its one fleet_feed_state row, a UUIDv7 that step 0 creates if it doesn't exist yet and that never changes with kinds open , source_read , alarm_write , handler . If storage can't be written at all, the failure is only logged; health then shows the object unavailable. No foreign key , because subjects live in several tables, some owned by agent-fleet-sync. Integrity: same-transaction create and delete, and health reports any row whose subject no longer exists (a UNION ALL over the subject tables).

Every subject is keyed by a UUIDv7 Your rule. How work runs: today vs the new design Today, almost every websocket request becomes a job, and a push waits in memory for its answer. The job waits for an alarm, the alarm runs cleanup first, and only then do jobs run, 8 at a time, each holding the object awake until its Router answers. In the new design a request is handled in the event that received it, an answer is its own event, and the object sleeps in between.

New: an object hibernating with its Routers connected sequenceDiagram participant R as Router participant P as Platform (Cloudflare edge) participant O as Fleet object R->>P: frame P->>O: build object if evicted; deliver frame O->>O: handle; due batch if allowed; set alarm or none Note over O: no timer, no waiter → idle P->>P: object hibernates; socket stays open; attachment kept R->>P: protocol Ping P-->>R: Pong (object not woken) Note over P: next frame or the alarm builds the object again from storage + attachments

The four kinds of work Kind When it runs How long If something fails 🟢 Answered now In the event that received the request Milliseconds, plus any object call it awaits (with a deadline) The request gets an error answer; nothing else is affected 🔵 Owed Sent at once when its receiver can take it; retried by its kind's rule ( four kinds ) Until done. Retries at 30 s, 1 min, 2 min… capped at 10 min. Mail kept up to 60 days; notices 7 days The row keeps its retry time and last error; health shows it stuck after 3 failed attempts 🟠 Due Selected at its due time; run by the next event, or the alarm if the object is quiet Up to 30 s of cadence after its time, then the platform's alarm delivery (not exact during maintenance); 500 items per source per batch That item gets a stored backoff in the failures table; everything else continues 🟣 Long operation In steps on durable-steps, unchanged until design 1 Seconds to minutes; each step bounded The engine retries the step. The engine runs at most 8 operations at once ( operation_engine.rs:20 ), so a ninth waits for a slot

Scratch sweep Scratch folders are created by collaboration-client ( acp_session_setup.rs:131–152 ), which runs in the Host and in other programs, so the Host's memory alone can't coordinate creating and removing (F8). Use is recorded in the folder. Creating or opening a scope, and closing a session on it, touch a .last-used file in the folder. Each day the sweep also touches it for every scope with a session open in the Host. So the folder's newest modification time covers use as well as writes, across restarts and shared thread folders. No database is added. Creating and removing never overlap. Both take a lock on scratch/.locks/<scope>.lock : creating or opening takes it shared for the moment of creation and touch; the sweep takes it exclusive, without waiting. Under the exclusive lock, the sweep rechecks that nothing changed for 30 days on the injected clock, renames the folder to a hidden name, releases the lock and deletes it. A creator that arrives later makes a fresh folder. A lock that can't be taken, or a folder whose state can't be read, is skipped. A failed removal is logged and retried the next day.

How one workflow runs on both engines sequenceDiagram participant E as Engine (Tokio, or the TS Workflow class) participant R as Rust replay executor participant B as Step body (Rust) loop until the run function returns E->>R: decide(event, saved results) R-->>E: next command: do "seal" / sleep / wait / complete alt do E->>B: run step body "seal" (attempt n) B-->>E: result E->>E: save result (Cloudflare: step.do saves it) else sleep / wait E->>E: saved wake time or event wait end end Tokio: three new tables (workflow instances, steps, events). Proposed home: inside each central object's existing SQLite store, where the old journal tables were. No new database file. Cloudflare: no database of ours. Cloudflare Workflows keeps instance state itself. It does add one new Worker ( collaboration-central-workflows ) and one Workflows binding per workflow. Effect receipts: an effect key → result record kept by each effect owner (Fleet, Copy, registry) beside the state it changes. Step budget Running decide as a step means a workflow with N body steps uses 2N + 1 Cloudflare steps. The public limit is 10,000 body steps (R11), so the Cloudflare Workflow is configured with its paid maximum of 25,000 steps, which covers 20,001. The Tokio engine counts body steps only, against the same 10,000, so both engines refuse the 10,001st body step the same way.

Cancellation, overlap and failure stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Preparing Preparing --> Invalid: admission refusal Preparing --> Unavailable: definition acquisition failure Preparing --> Running: admitted run Preparing --> Valid: valid check Preparing --> Settling: abort Running --> Settling: terminal result or abort Settling --> Completed: owned work settled Settling --> Cancelled: cancellation settled Settling --> Incomplete: partial failure settled Preparing --> Failed: detectable adapter failure Settling --> Failed: unknown native reply Valid --> [*] Unavailable --> [*] Failed --> [*] Invalid --> [*] Completed --> [*] Cancelled --> [*] Incomplete --> [*] An already-aborted signal wins before encoding/native dispatch and returns cancelled. A cancellation observed before execution starts prevents new work; a cancellation during execution cancels only that call and awaits owned settlement. Partial reports retain only actual work. Each call has its own explicit repository/base paths, cancellation token, limits and backend context. Concurrent calls never change process CWD or overwrite shared environment to select a model/key. Any shared backend scheduler follows existing Rust request/concurrency limits rather than a second SDK queue. Failure / overlap Owner and behavior Retry / recovery Missing/malformed definition or graph/reference error Capture/admission returns typed unavailable/invalid diagnostics with real origin. No backend is acquired by check. Caller edits or reloads explicitly; no fabricated defaults. Unsupported function/cycle/non-finite/unsafe numeric value SDK encoder returns failed/encoding_rejected before dispatch. bigint uses lossless internal encoding; Rust rejects range/nonzero violations. Caller repairs values; no lossy coercion. Incompatible addon contract Lazy native loader returns failed before engine effects; generated wrapper compares SDK release and contract revision. Reinstall a matching pinned package; no automatic downgrade. Provider refusal/timeout or partial engine work Existing backend/executor policies decide retries within one engine call; RunOutcome retains incomplete evidence. SDK adds no whole-run retry. Caller may explicitly start a new call; no claim of inference idempotency. Two calls, one aborted Per-call tokens/contexts isolate all mutable run state; native task awaits settlement. Other call proceeds; pre-dispatch abort starts no work. Native process crash No typed successful response is fabricated. A fatal in-process addon crash may terminate Node; no caught exception or returned outcome is promised. Detectable native-call/reply failures return failed, with effects unknown after dispatch. No persistence/recovery engine or replay is invented.

The adapter lazily loads the native addon on a call, so an unsupported addon is a typed call failure; a package-manager installation failure remains an installation diagnostic. diagnostics: readonly Diagnostic[] } | { kind: 'unavailable'; diagnostics: readonly Diagnostic[] } | { kind: 'cancelled'; diagnostics: readonly Diagnostic[] } | { kind: 'failed'; failure: SdkFailure }; report: IncompleteReport } | { kind: 'cancelled'; report: CancelledReport | null } | { kind: 'failed'; failure: SdkFailure; report: SdkReport | null }; type SdkFailure = | { phase: 'before_dispatch'; effects: 'none'; reason: 'unsupported_runtime' | 'unsupported_platform' | 'addon_missing' | 'contract_mismatch' | 'encoding_rejected'; message: string } | { phase: 'after_dispatch'; effects: 'unknown'; Provider and engine work that has partial results uses incomplete, not unavailable. A failed outcome after dispatch says effects are unknown even after local tasks settle; it must not trigger a transparent retry. Fatal process termination is outside returned outcomes. An unexpected prepared reply is failed/native_reply_invalid, never fabricated as a completed inference. CompletedReport, InvalidReport, IncompleteReport and CancelledReport are generated Rust DTO variants with their status narrowed to the indicated values. 1. Choose a machine and session The UX client identifies a Host and a continuing execution session. The Gateway routes to that Host. Host identity is part of the target; an unavailable Host must not silently redirect the operation to another machine.

4. Prepare an exact output attempt The Host annotation workflow prepares the selected immutable output bytes and attempt metadata. The Gateway routes and exposes the authorized result.
